nodes.title: Density of eigenfunctions and injectivity into D(G, ℚ_p)_λ
nodes.statement: Let λ be an induced infinitesimal character. Then C^la(G, ℚ_p)[λ] is dense in C(G, ℚ_p) for the supremum norm, and consequently the composite ℚ_p[[G]] → D(G, ℚ_p) → D(G, ℚ_p)_λ is injective.
hypotheses: Only induced λ are treated by this argument; for non-induced integral λ injectivity is proved through Verma modules (ND.5/central-injectivity-theorem).
proofSteps: f_0·C^sm(G, ℚ_p) ⊆ C^la(G, ℚ_p)[λ] (ND.5/principal-series-eigenfunction); since f_0 is a unit of C(G, ℚ_p) and C^sm(G, ℚ_p) is dense in C(G, ℚ_p), so is f_0·C^sm(G, ℚ_p) (Fu, proof of Theorem 5.2, p. 17).

ℚ_p[[G]] is the continuous dual of C(G, ℚ_p) (bounded measures, PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras L0–L1). A measure μ whose image in D(G, ℚ_p)_λ = (C^la[λ])′_b (ND.5/central-strong-duality) vanishes kills the dense subspace C^la[λ], hence μ = 0.
acceptance: For λ = λ_0 = 0 (χ trivial), the function f_0 = 1 already shows that the locally constant functions lie in C^la[0].

sources.locator: Theorem 5.2, second assertion, and its proof, pp. 16–17
sources.match: Proves that for induced λ the composite ℚ_p[[G]] → D(G, ℚ_p) ⊗_{Z(g), λ} ℚ_p is injective, by density of f_0·C^sm(G, ℚ_p) in C(G, ℚ_p).

nodes.title: Central specialisation commutes with the Banach steps
nodes.statement: In the setting of ND.5/infinitesimal-character-quotients with G = G_1^m (p odd) and r_n = p^{−1/p^n}, the natural map D(G, ℚ_p)_λ → lim_n D^λ_{r_n}(G, ℚ_p) is an isomorphism of Fréchet algebras.
hypotheses: The isomorphism is not formal (tensor products do not commute with inverse limits in general); it uses coadmissibility of the central quotient.
proofSteps: I = D(G, ℚ_p)·ker λ is a closed two-sided ideal (ND.5/infinitesimal-character-quotients), so ST03 Proposition 3.7 (ND.2/coadmissible-theorems) gives D/I ≅ lim_n D_{r_n}/D_{r_n}I, and D_{r_n}I = D_{r_n}·ker λ because ker λ is generated by central elements; the r_n are cofinal in p^ℚ ∩ (1/p, 1).

Fu's proof instead dualises: by Theorem 5.2, D_λ ≅ (C^la[λ])′_b = lim_n (C^{n,an}[λ])′_b, and the deep translation estimate ‖g − 1‖ ≤ 1/p on C^{n,an}(G, ℚ_p) for g ∈ G^{p^{n+1}} gives maps D_{r_{n+1}} → (C^{n,an})′_b (Fu (28)–(29)); both routes give the same map on Dirac distributions.
acceptance: For λ = λ_k each D^λ_{r_n} surjects onto End(W_k), compatibly in n.

sources.locator: Proposition 5.5 and its proof, with the estimate preceding (29), pp. 18–19
sources.match: Proves D(G, ℚ_p) ⊗_{Z(g), λ} ℚ_p ≅ lim_n D^λ_{r_n}(G, ℚ_p) by strong duality and the action of D_{r_{n+1}} on the Banach spaces C^{n,an}(G, ℚ_p).

sources.locator: Proposition 3.7 and its proof, pp. 11–12
sources.match: For a closed two-sided ideal I of a Fréchet–Stein algebra, A/I ≅ lim_n A_{q_n}/A_{q_n}I.

nodes.title: Central quotients D^λ_r(G_1^m, ℚ_p) are domains for integral λ
nodes.statement: Let p be odd, G = G_1^m, λ ∈ ℤ_p^m and 1/p < r < 1. Put Δ′_i = p²Δ_i, expressed in the coordinates F_i, H_i, E_i (ND.0/first-congruence-sl2) through pf_i = log(1 + F_i), ph_i = log(1 + H_i), pe_i = log(1 + E_i). (i) For 1/p < r′ < p^{−1/2}, the principal symbol of Δ′_i − p²λ_i for the norm ‖·‖_{r′} is ½H_i² + 2E_iF_i, and gr_{r′} D_{r′}(G, ℚ_p)/(Δ′_i − p²λ_i)_i ≅ 𝔽_p[ε, ε⁻¹][F_i, H_i, E_i]/(½H_i² + 2E_iF_i)_i, an integral domain. (ii) Consequently D^λ_r(G, ℚ_p) is an integral domain for every 1/p < r < p^{−1/2} (taking r′ = r). (iii) For p^{−1/2} ≤ r < 1, in particular for the radii r_n = p^{−1/p^n} used in ND.5/fu-direct-injectivity, the same conclusion holds provided the filtration induced by ‖·‖_{r′} on D_r/D_r·ker λ is separated, i.e. D_r ∩ D_{r′}·ker λ = D_r·ker λ inside D_{r′}; this separatedness is a recorded gap. For p ≥ 5 the radii p^{−1/2} ≤ r < p^{−1/(p−1)} are covered directly by ND.5/small-radius-central, so the open range is p^{−1/(p−1)} ≤ r < 1, which contains every r_n. (iv) For non-integral parameters the statement fails: for r = p^{−2/3} and λ(Δ) = p^{−1}, D^λ_r(G_1, ℚ_p) = 0.
hypotheses: Integrality of λ (v_p(p²λ) ≥ 2) is necessary: Fu Theorem 5.7 states the domain property for all λ and all 1/p < r < 1 (sourceIssues E7).

At the radius r = r_n itself the direct graded argument fails: there the logarithm log(1 + X) has principal symbol p^{−n}σ(X)^{p^n}, so the symbol of p²Δ − p²λ for ‖·‖_{r_n} is a unit times (½H² + 2EF)^{p^n} (Frobenius is additive in characteristic p), and the graded ring of D^λ_{r_n} has nilpotents. This is why the source passes to a weaker norm.
proofSteps: gr_{r′} D_{r′}(G_1, ℚ_p) ≅ 𝔽_p[ε, ε⁻¹][F, H, E] (ND.2/banach-step-structure, using ST03 Theorem 4.5 under (HYP)), and for r′ < p^{−1/2} the logarithms log(1 + X) have principal symbol X, since max_k r′^k/|k| = r′ (Fu, proof of Theorem 5.7).

p²Δ − p²λ = ½(log(1 + H))² − p log(1 + H) + 2 log(1 + E) log(1 + F) − p²λ has symbol ½H² + 2EF when v_p(p²λ) ≥ 2; ½H² + 2EF is irreducible over the algebraic closure (it is a nondegenerate quadratic form in three variables), so the quotient of the polynomial ring is a domain, also for products (Fu Lemma 3.3, third part).

Fu Lemma 2.2 identifies gr of A/A·a with gr A/gr a when gr a is regular; with a separated induced filtration this transfers the domain property from the graded ring to D^λ_r. For r′ = r < p^{−1/2} separatedness holds because the ideal is closed (finitely generated in a noetherian Banach algebra, ST03 Proposition 2.1).
(iv): ‖Δ‖_r ≤ p^{2/3} < p = |λ| makes Δ − λ = −λ(1 − Δ/λ) a unit by the geometric series.
acceptance: For λ = λ_k and r < p^{−1/2}, D^{λ_k}_r(G_1, ℚ_p) is a domain surjecting onto End(W_k) for k ≥ 1 — a domain with a matrix-algebra quotient, which is consistent because the kernel is a nonzero two-sided ideal.

sources.locator: Theorem 5.7 and its proof, p. 20, with Lemma 2.2, p. 6, and Lemma 3.3, p. 9
sources.match: Shows that D^λ_r(G, ℚ_p) is an integral domain by computing its graded ring for a weaker norm ‖·‖_{r′}, r′ < p^{−1/2}, and identifying the symbol of p²Δ + λ_0 with ½H² + 2EF.

nodes.title: Small radii: logarithmic coordinates and central quotients
nodes.statement: Let p be odd, G = G_1^m and p^{−1} ≤ r < p^{−1/(p−1)}, any real radius; put ρ = pr. (i) The map e_i, f_i, h_i ↦ p^{−1} log(1 + E_i), p^{−1} log(1 + F_i), p^{−1} log(1 + H_i) extends to an isometric isomorphism of Banach algebras from the completion B_ρ of U(sl_2(ℤ_p)^m) ⊗ ℚ_p for the weighted PBW norm |Σ c_α x^α|_ρ = sup |c_α| ρ^{|α|} onto D_r(G, ℚ_p), with inverse given on group coordinates by b_i ↦ exp(p x_i) − 1. (ii) For λ ∈ ℤ_p^m the ideal D_r·ker λ is closed and D^λ_r(G, ℚ_p) is a nonzero integral domain, with an explicit normal form: every element is uniquely Σ_α d_α Π_i e_i^{a_i} f_i^{b_i} h_i^{c_i} with c_i ∈ {0, 1} and |d_α| ρ^{|α|} → 0, and the quotient norm is attained on normal forms.
hypotheses: This is a derived statement, not printed in the source: it combines Fu's equations (27) and (30) with the convergence of log and exp on the stated range; no rationality of log_p r is needed.
It does not cover the radii r_n = p^{−1/p^n} ≥ p^{−1/p}, which exceed p^{−1/(p−1)}.
proofSteps: For r < p^{−1/(p−1)}, ‖log(1 + b) − b‖_r < ‖b‖_r and exp(px) − 1 converges, so log(1 + b_i) and b_i have the same norm r and the coordinate changes are mutually inverse isometries (compare Fu (27) and (30)); the ρ = pr normalisation accounts for x = p^{−1} log(1 + b).

Normal form: in B_ρ divide by Δ − λ using h² = 2(Δ − λ) + 2λ + 2h − 4ef; for |λ| ≤ 1 ≤ ρ² each reduction step does not increase the weighted norm, so division has bounded quotient and remainder, the ideal is closed and the normal forms give a topological basis (cf. Fu Lemma 3.3, first part, for the algebraic basis).

Domain: for ρ > 1 the graded ring for |·|_ρ is 𝔽_p[ε, ε⁻¹][e, f, h]/(½h² + 2ef) (rescaled), a domain, and the ideal is closed, so the induced filtration is separated and Fu Lemma 2.2 transfers the domain property; at ρ = 1 (r = 1/p) the quotient is Û(sl_2(ℤ_p)^m)_λ, a domain by Fu Lemma 3.3 (last part).
acceptance: At r = p^{−1}, ρ = 1 and B_1 = Û(sl_2(ℤ_p)^m)_{ℚ_p}, recovering ND.4/d-one-over-p for G_1^m.

sources.locator: §5, equations (27) and (30), pp. 17 and 20; Lemma 3.3, p. 9
sources.match: Gives Frommer's description of U_r(g) in logarithmic coordinates, the identification x ↦ log(1 + (x − 1)) of the Lie action, and the basis e^a f^b h^c (c ∈ {0, 1}) of U(sl_2)/(Δ − r).

nodes.title: Ext and grade over a finite crossed product
nodes.statement: Let T = R ∗ H be a crossed product of a ring R by a finite group H and M a right T-module. Then Ext^i_T(M, T) ≅ Ext^i_R(M, R) as left R-modules for all i ≥ 0; the left-module version holds by passing to opposite rings. Consequently, if R and T are noetherian (Auslander–Gorenstein), the grade j_T(M) = inf{i : Ext^i_T(M, T) ≠ 0} equals j_R(M), and the injective dimensions of R and T agree.
proofSteps: Ext^i_T(−, T) and Ext^i_R(−, R) are derived from Hom_T(−, T) and Hom_R(−, R); T is free of finite rank over R, so projective T-resolutions restrict to projective R-resolutions, and it suffices to show T ≅ Hom_R(T_R, R_R) as right T-modules (AB07 §5.4 Lemma, proof).
The isomorphism is α(f) = Σ_{g∈H} f(ḡ) ḡ⁻¹, with inverse β(Σ r_g ḡ)(h̄) = r_{h⁻¹}: the coefficient-of-identity Frobenius pairing (AB07 p. 17).
acceptance: For H trivial the statement is a tautology; for R a field and T = R[H] (trivial action and twisting), Ext^i_{R[H]}(M, R[H]) ≅ Ext^i_R(M, R) = 0 for i > 0, reflecting that group algebras of finite groups are self-injective.

sources.locator: §5.4, Lemma and its proof, and the Corollary, pp. 16–17
sources.match: Proves Ext^i_T(M, T) ≅ Ext^i_R(M, R) for a crossed product T = R ∗ G with G finite, via T ≅ Hom_R(T, R), and deduces equality of injective dimensions.

sources.locator: §5, proof of Theorem 5.1, p. 21
sources.match: Applies [AB07, Cor 5.4] to compare codimensions of D^λ_r/δD^λ_r over D^λ_r and over U^λ_r.

nodes.title: Topological PBW normal form of U^λ_r(g) and its injection into Û(g)_λ
nodes.statement: Let p be odd, G = G_1^m, λ ∈ ℤ_p^m and r = r_n (n ≥ 1). Then U_{r_n}(g) is the weighted completion of U(sl_2(ℤ_p)^m) ⊗ ℚ_p for the PBW weight p^n on each of e_i, f_i, h_i; every element of U^λ_{r_n}(g) is uniquely a convergent sum Σ_α d_α Π_i e_i^{a_i} f_i^{b_i} h_i^{c_i} with c_i ∈ {0, 1} and |d_α|·p^{n|α|} → 0; U^λ_{r_n}(g) is an integral domain; and the natural map U^λ_{r_n}(g) → Û(g)_λ is injective, Û(g)_λ having the same normal forms with weight 1.
hypotheses: The source leaves this normal form to the reader; the bounded division below supplies it. Separatedness of the quotient topology and the injection are proved together from the normal form, never by assuming the injection.
proofSteps: Frommer's description (ND.3/frommer-theorem) with x_i = log(g_i) ∈ {ph_i, pe_i, pf_i} and ‖x_i‖_{r_n} = p^{n−1} (ND.3/crossed-product-radius) shows that U_{r_n}(g) consists of Σ c_α e^a f^b h^c with |c_α| p^{n|α|} → 0, i.e. the weighted completion with weight p^n.

Bounded division by Δ_i − λ_i: replace h_i² by 2(Δ_i − λ_i) + 2λ_i + 2h_i − 4e_if_i; with weight ρ = p^n ≥ 1 and |λ_i| ≤ 1 no reduction step increases the weighted norm, so every element has a unique normal form with remainder bounded by the norm, the ideal is closed and the quotient norm is the sup norm on normal forms (Fu Lemma 3.3, first part, for the algebraic basis of U(sl_2)/(Δ − λ)).
Domain: the graded ring for the weighted norm is 𝔽_p[ε, ε⁻¹][e_i, f_i, h_i]/(½h_i² + 2e_if_i), a domain (Fu Lemma 3.3, third part, and Lemma 2.2).
Injectivity: the inclusion of the weight-p^n completion into the weight-1 completion Û(g) maps normal forms to normal forms with the same coefficients.
acceptance: For λ = λ_k the normal form of U^λ_r(g) maps onto End(W_k); the kernel is the ideal of normal forms vanishing on W_k.

nodes.title: Injectivity of central specialisation for induced characters (direct route)
nodes.statement: Let p be odd, G = G_1^m and λ an induced infinitesimal character. Then the composite ℚ_p[[G]] → Û(g_{ℚ_p}) → Û(g)_λ of the microlocalisation (ND.4/lazard-microlocalisation) and central specialisation is injective.
hypotheses: This route depends on ND.5/radius-central-domain at the radii r_n, whose proof has a recorded gap (separatedness); the theorem itself, and its extension to all λ ∈ ℤ_p^m, are established independently by ND.5/central-injectivity-theorem.
proofSteps: For 0 ≠ δ ∈ ℚ_p[[G]], its image in D(G, ℚ_p)_λ is nonzero (ND.5/eigenspace-density-injectivity), so by ND.5/central-projective-limit its image in D^λ_{r_n} is nonzero for some n.

D^λ_{r_n} is a noetherian domain (ND.5/radius-central-domain, with its gap) and Auslander–Gorenstein (its graded ring is a commutative hypersurface; AW13 Proposition 2.5(b)), so the torsion module D^λ_{r_n}/δD^λ_{r_n} has positive grade (AW13 Proposition 2.5(a), condition (iii) of an exact dimension function).

D^λ_{r_n} = U^λ_{r_n} ∗ (G/G^{p^n}) (ND.3/crossed-product-radius), so the grade over U^λ_{r_n} is the same (ND.5/crossed-product-ext-comparison). If U^λ_{r_n} ∩ δD^λ_{r_n} were 0, U^λ_{r_n} would embed in D^λ_{r_n}/δD^λ_{r_n}, contradicting grade j(U^λ_{r_n}) = 0; hence there is δ′ with 0 ≠ δδ′ ∈ U^λ_{r_n}.
U^λ_{r_n} → Û(g)_λ is injective (ND.5/central-radius-normal-form), and Û(g) = D_{1/p}(G, ℚ_p) (ND.4/d-one-over-p), so the image of δδ′, hence of δ, in Û(g)_λ is nonzero.
acceptance: For m = 1 and λ = λ_k = ½k(k + 2) (induced by χ(t) = t^k), every nonzero δ ∈ ℚ_p[[G_1]] has nonzero image in Û(g)_{λ_k}, although its image in End(W_k) may vanish.

nodes.title: Integral Casimir parameters come from integral highest weights after a finite extension
nodes.statement: Let p be odd and λ = (λ_1, …, λ_m) ∈ ℤ_p^m. Let K = ℚ_p(√(1 + 2λ_1), …, √(1 + 2λ_m)), a finite extension of degree at most 2^m, with integers R. Then a_i := −1 + √(1 + 2λ_i) ∈ R satisfies a_i(a_i + 2)/2 = λ_i, so the R-linear character a : t_0 = ⊕ ℤ_p h_i → R, h_i ↦ a_i, has central character χ_a(Δ_i) = λ_i on the affinoid Verma module of highest weight a. The extension K is in general ramified or nontrivial even when λ_i ∈ ℤ_p: λ is induced over ℚ_p (ND.5/induced-infinitesimal-characters) only when every √(1 + 2λ_i) ∈ ℤ_p.
proofSteps: a_i is a root of the monic polynomial X² + 2X − 2λ_i ∈ ℤ_p[X], hence integral over ℤ_p; a_i(a_i + 2)/2 = ((a_i + 1)² − 1)/2 = λ_i.
On a highest weight vector v (e_iv = 0, h_iv = a_iv), Δ_iv = (½a_i² − a_i + 2e_if_i)v = (½a_i² − a_i + 2a_i)v = ½a_i(a_i + 2)v, using e_if_i = f_ie_i + h_i.
acceptance: At p = 3 and λ = 1, K = ℚ_3(√3) is ramified and a = −1 + √3 ∈ ℤ_3[√3].

nodes.title: Affinoid Verma modules are faithful over Iwasawa algebras
nodes.statement: Let p be odd, L/ℚ_p finite, K a complete discretely valued extension of L with integers R, 𝔾 a connected simply connected split semisimple group scheme over o_L with Lie algebra 𝔤, p very good for 𝔾, and G an L-uniform group with p^n 𝔤 = R ⊗ (1/p) L_G (for example the congruence kernel ker(𝔾(o_L) → 𝔾(o_L/p^{n+1}))). For an R-linear character λ : p^n t → R, the affinoid Verma module V̂^λ = Û(𝔤)_{n,K} ⊗_{Û(b⁺)_{n,K}} K_λ satisfies: (i) its annihilator in Û(𝔤)_{n,K} is the two-sided ideal generated by ker(χ_λ : Z(𝔤_K) → K); (ii) V̂^λ is faithful as a K[[G]]-module. Hence K[[G]] → Û(𝔤)_{n,K}/Û(𝔤)_{n,K}·ker χ_λ is injective. For 𝔾 = SL_2^m over ℤ_p and G = G_1^m one has n = 0 (ND.0/first-congruence-sl2), and every p odd is very good.
hypotheses: Simply connected and very good p are hypotheses of AW14 §4.4–4.6 and §5.4; for type A_1 very good means p ∤ 2.
proofSteps: (i): Ch(V̂^λ) = (b⁺_k)^⊥; the ideal Gr(ker χ_λ·Û) is S(𝔤_k)^{G_k}_+·S(𝔤_k), prime, with zero set the nilpotent cone 𝒩^*; the annihilator is G(R)-stable, so its characteristic variety contains G·(b⁺_k)^⊥, dense in 𝒩^*; primality forces equality of graded ideals (AW14 Lemma and Theorem 4.6, p. 11).

(ii): V̂^λ is free of rank one over Û(p^n n)_K; the action of R T on U(n_K)v is faithful (AW14 Proposition 4.7), so V̂^λ is faithful over R B by the general faithfulness theorem 5.3, then over R B⁺ by the Cartan involution (Proposition 4.8), and finally over K[[G]] by Theorem 5.3 again (AW14 Theorem 5.4, proof, p. 16).
The injectivity statement is the composite of (ii) with (i).
acceptance: For G_1 ⊂ SL_2(ℤ_p) and λ = k ∈ ℕ, V̂^k has the finite-dimensional quotient Sym^k, but V̂^k itself is infinite-dimensional and faithful over ℚ_p[[G_1]], whereas Sym^k is not faithful.

sources.match: Computes the annihilator of affinoid Verma modules as generated by the kernel of the central character, and proves that affinoid Verma modules are faithful over KG for congruence kernels of simply connected split semisimple groups at very good odd p, including n = 0.

nodes.title: Injectivity of central specialisation for every integral parameter
nodes.statement: Let p be odd, G = G_1^m = Π (I_2 + pM_2(ℤ_p)) ∩ SL_2(ℤ_p) and g = sl_2(ℚ_p)^m with Casimirs Δ_1, …, Δ_m. For every λ ∈ ℤ_p^m the composite ℚ_p[[G]] → Û(g_{ℤ_p})_{ℚ_p} → Û(g)_λ = Û(g_{ℤ_p})_{ℚ_p}/(Δ_i − λ_i)_i of the microlocalisation and central specialisation is injective. Equivalently, the image of every nonzero element of ℚ_p[[G]] in Û(g) is generic: it stays nonzero in Û(g)_λ for all λ ∈ ℤ_p^m.
hypotheses: λ is arbitrary in ℤ_p^m, including parameters not induced over ℚ_p; the proof passes through a finite extension of coefficients and descends.
proofSteps: Choose K and integral a_i with a_i(a_i + 2)/2 = λ_i (ND.5/integral-casimir-roots).
By ND.5/affinoid-verma-faithfulness with n = 0, K[[G]] → Û(g_R)_K/(Δ_i − λ_i) is injective.

Descent: K[[G]] = K ⊗_{ℚ_p} ℚ_p[[G]], Û(g_R)_K = K ⊗_{ℚ_p} Û(g_{ℤ_p})_{ℚ_p} (ND.3/completed-enveloping-algebra, base change) and the quotient by the central ideal commutes with K ⊗ −; the square formed by the two microlocalisation maps commutes (ND.4/microlocal-coefficient-extension). K is faithfully flat over ℚ_p, so the kernel of the ℚ_p-map is zero once its K-base change is.
For induced λ this is also ND.5/fu-direct-injectivity, which Fu proves directly.
acceptance: For m = 1, λ = 0: ℚ_p[[G_1]] embeds into Û(sl_2(ℤ_p))_{ℚ_p}/(Δ), the completed algebra of the Casimir-zero quotient, though the target has dimension 2 (in the sense of its characteristic variety) against 3 for ℚ_p[[G_1]].
At p = 3, λ = 1 (not induced) the statement still holds, through K = ℚ_3(√3).

nodes.title: Admissible Banach representations and finitely generated Iwasawa modules
nodes.statement: Let K be a finite extension of ℚ_p with integers o and G a compact p-adic Lie group (so o[[G]] and K[[G]] = K ⊗_o o[[G]] are noetherian). (i) A finitely generated o[[G]]-module carries a unique Hausdorff topology, its canonical topology, for which the action is continuous; submodules are closed and o[[G]]-linear maps continuous. (ii) A K-Banach representation E of G is admissible if there is a G-invariant bounded open o-lattice L ⊆ E such that (E/L)^H is of cofinite type for every open normal subgroup H; E is admissible iff its continuous dual E′ is finitely generated over K[[G]], with K[[G]] acting by the contragredient action through bounded measures. (iii) The functor M ↦ M^d := Hom_o^{cont}(M_0, K) (for a finitely generated o-torsion-free lattice M_0 of M, with the canonical topology) is an anti-equivalence between finitely generated K[[G]]-modules and admissible K-Banach representations of G, quasi-inverse to E ↦ E′; in particular the admissible representations form an abelian category. (iv) Under (iii), finite-dimensional continuous representations W correspond to finite-dimensional K[[G]]-modules W′ (the dual), and Hom_{K[[G]]}(M, W) ≅ Hom_G(W′, M^d) for finitely generated M.
hypotheses: K is a finite extension of ℚ_p (more generally discretely valued with o noetherian); G compact p-adic Lie, so that o[[G]] is noetherian (NoncommutativeAndEquivariantIwasawa:NE.0/iwasawa-noetherian).

The duality is Schikhof duality between compact o-modules and Banach spaces with lattices, not the strong duality of locally analytic distributions; the two are compared through ND.1/iwasawa-to-distributions.
proofSteps: (i): o[[G]] is compact and noetherian, so a finite presentation gives the canonical topology (ST02B Proposition 3.1).

(ii): if E′ is finitely generated, its unit ball is a finitely generated compact o[[G]]-module and the cofinite-type condition follows from topological Nakayama (NoncommutativeAndEquivariantIwasawa:NE.0/compact-nakayama); conversely the cofinite-type condition makes the Pontryagin dual of E/L a finitely generated o[[G]]-module (ST02B Lemma 3.4).

(iii): the anti-equivalence between o-torsion-free compact o[[G]]-modules up to isogeny and Banach representations (ST02B Theorem 2.3) is the G-equivariant form of Schikhof duality; its biduality isomorphisms for torsion-free compact o-modules and for o-lattices are planned in CompletedCohomologyPartII:CC.3/qualified-biduality and imported from there. Restricted by (i)–(ii) it gives ST02B Theorem 3.5.
(iv) is the restriction of (iii) to finite-dimensional objects together with adjunction.
acceptance: For G = ℤ_p and E = C(ℤ_p, K) (left regular representation), E′ = K[[ℤ_p]] is free of rank one.
Fu §6: the dual of K[[G]] as a module over itself is C(G, K), and W_k^* ≅ W_k is a finite-dimensional K[[G]]-module.

nodes.title: Algebraic functions on a compact open subgroup of SL₂(ℤ_p)
nodes.statement: Let G ⊆ SL_2(ℤ_p) be an open subgroup (in particular G_1) and K/ℚ_p finite. The algebraic functions on G are C^alg(G, K) := the image of K[SL_2] = K[x, y, z, w]/(xw − yz − 1) under restriction to G (via g = (x y; z w)); restriction K[SL_2] → C(G, K) is injective, so C^alg(G, K) ≅ K[SL_2]. G × G acts by left and right translation, (g_1, g_2)·f(g) = f(g_1⁻¹ g g_2), preserving the degree filtration C^alg_{≤n} (images of polynomials of total degree ≤ n in x, y, z, w). dim_K C^alg_{≤n}/C^alg_{≤n−1} = C(n+3, 3) − C(n+1, 3) = (n + 1)². For G = G_1^m use the tensor product of the factors.
hypotheses: Injectivity of restriction uses Zariski density of the open subgroup G in SL_2 over K (an open subgroup of a connected group's ℚ_p-points is Zariski dense); it fails for finite subgroups.
proofSteps: A polynomial vanishing on an open subset of SL_2(ℚ_p) vanishes identically, since SL_2 is an irreducible variety and an open subgroup is Zariski dense (it contains a neighbourhood of 1, where an analytic chart shows any regular function vanishing is zero).
The degree-n piece of K[x, y, z, w] modulo the degree-n piece of (xw − yz − 1)·K[x, y, z, w]_{≤n−2} has dimension C(n+3, 3) − C(n+1, 3) = (n + 1)² (Fu §6, p. 22).
acceptance: n = 0: constants, dimension 1; n = 1: the span of x, y, z, w modulo constants, dimension 4.

nodes.title: The algebraic Peter–Weyl theorem on a compact open subgroup of SL₂
nodes.statement: Let p be odd, G = G_1^m, k ∈ ℕ^m, W_k = ⊠_i Sym^{k_i}(K²) and K/ℚ_p finite. (i) W_k, restricted to any open subgroup of G, is absolutely irreducible, self-dual (W_k^* ≅ W_k), its differentiated action is the algebraic sl_2^m-action, and it is a Lie module (ND.4/lie-module-of-representation). (ii) For m = 1, C^alg_{≤k}/C^alg_{≤k−1} ≅ W_k ⊗ W_k^* as G × G-representations, and the W_k-isotypic algebraic vectors in C(G, K) (for either the left or the right action) form a closed subspace isomorphic to W_k ⊗ W_k^*; for m ≥ 1 the same holds for the tensor products. (iii) Under the duality of ND.6/banach-iwasawa-duality, the maximal W_k-quotient of K[[G]] is K[[G]]/Ann_{K[[G]]}(W_k) ≅ End_K(W_k), so dim_K Hom_{K[[G]]}(K[[G]], W_k) = dim W_k = Π (k_i + 1).
hypotheses: Irreducibility on every open subgroup uses Zariski density, or the Lie-module comparison; irreducibility for an arbitrary (for example finite) subgroup is false.
proofSteps: (i): an open subgroup is Zariski dense in SL_2^m, so its invariant subspaces in the algebraic representation W_k are sl_2^m-stable, and W_k is irreducible under sl_2^m (LieHighestWeight Layer 0); self-duality is the invariant pairing on Sym^k; W_k is a Lie module because it is the restriction of an algebraic representation (AW13 Theorem 11.3 factorisation with trivial Artin factor; Fu §6, p. 22).

(ii): x^k, as a function of g = (x y; z w), is left-invariant under the lower unipotent and right-invariant under the upper unipotent subgroup with highest weight k, and generates a copy of W_k ⊗ W_k^* in degree k; the dimension count (k + 1)² of ND.6/algebraic-matrix-coefficients gives equality; complete reducibility identifies the isotypic algebraic vectors (Fu §6, pp. 21–22); finite-dimensional subspaces are closed.

(iii): the duality of ND.6/banach-iwasawa-duality identifies the maximal W_k-quotient of K[[G]] with the dual of the W_k-isotypic part of C(G, K), which is W_k ⊗ W_k^*; hence K[[G]]/Ann(W_k) ≅ End(W_k) (Fu (32)); alternatively (32) follows from ND.4/isotypic-comparison.
acceptance: k = 0: the maximal trivial quotient of K[[G]] is K (augmentation), End(W_0) = K.
k = 1, m = 1: K[[G_1]]/Ann(K²) ≅ M_2(K), of dimension 4 = (1 + 1)².

gaps.title: Separatedness of the weaker-norm filtration on central quotients at large radii
gaps.detail: Fu's proof of Theorem 5.7 computes gr_{r′} of D_r/D_r(p²Δ + λ_0) for a weaker norm ‖·‖_{r′}, r′ < p^{−1/2}, and needs the induced filtration to be separated, i.e. D_r ∩ D_{r′}·(p²Δ − p²λ) = D_r·(p²Δ − p²λ) inside D_{r′}. It holds for r < p^{−1/2} (take r′ = r), and ND.5/small-radius-central gives the domain property directly for r < p^{−1/(p−1)}; at the radius r_n itself the graded ring of D^λ_{r_n} is not a domain (the symbol of p²Δ − p²λ is a p^n-th power), so the weaker norm cannot be avoided. The radii r_n = p^{−1/p^n} used in the proof of Theorem 5.1 all exceed p^{−1/2}. Density of D_r in D_{r′} and the domain property of the graded ring do not imply separatedness. restructure.detail: The design brief joins three continuations of LocallyAnalyticDistributions.
